transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Yeah, um... so the main thing that really pushed me to finally make an appointment and come in today is... well, it's my job. I work as an insurance claims clerk, and it's, you know, a desk job. Lots of sitting. But I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, all the time. And it's becoming a real problem because even when I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish my claim reviews—which is literally my entire job, just sitting there going through these policies and claims—I just can't seem to stay in my chair. 

I'll tell myself, 'Okay, just sit here and finish this batch,' but then five minutes later I'm up. I'm walking to the water cooler, or pacing over by the printer even if I didn't print anything, or just kind of wandering down the hall. And I know I shouldn't be doing it, I know my supervisor expects me to be at my desk working through the queue, but it's like I just have to get up. And then, of course, the claims just pile up, which stresses me out, but I still keep walking away from my desk even when I have a mountain of paperwork staring right at me. It's just getting really frustrating to deal with every single day.
Can you tell me whether you've experienced this kind of restlessness and difficulty staying seated since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Well, um... if I really think about it, looking back, this whole thing... it wasn’t really brand new for me. I mean, I guess it looked a little different when I was a kid, but the core of it was definitely there. 

Like, going all the way back to elementary school, I remember my parents used to keep all my old report cards in this big accordion folder in the office, and whenever they had parent-teacher conferences, it was always the exact same conversation. Every single year, without fail. My teachers used to write these long notes in the comments section—and they were always so specific—saying that I was a really bright kid, which, you know, my mom always loved to hear. But then there was always a "but." 

They would write that I constantly lost my worksheets. I would literally just get a handout passed to me, and five minutes later it was completely gone, shoved in the back of my desk or crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack. And they always, always mentioned that I missed instructions. The teacher could be standing right at the front of the room explaining exactly what we were supposed to be doing for a science project or whatever, and I would just completely miss it. I don't know where my head was, but I just wouldn't absorb what they were saying. And they always said I needed constant reminders just to finish my basic classwork. I'd do the first two questions of an assignment and then just sort of drift off or start messing with my pencils, and they'd have to physically come over and tap on my desk to get me to finish what was right in front of me. 

So, yeah, I guess struggling to just sit there and actually do the work I'm supposed to do has been happening pretty much my whole life. It's just that now it's insurance claims instead of spelling worksheets, you know?

When you notice yourself getting up and unable to stay seated, are you also experiencing a lot of worry or anxious thoughts running through your mind at that time, or is it more just a physical urge to move without particular worries attached?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because my girlfriend actually asked me something really similar the other day when I was complaining about how much trouble I'm having at the office. She was like, 'Are you stressed about the claims? Are you having anxiety about the workload?' But honestly... no, not really. 

It’s not like my mind is racing with all these worst-case scenarios or anything like that. I’m not sitting there at my desk worrying about, you know, my bills, or getting fired, or even the fact that I'm behind on my work—well, I mean, I *do* worry about being behind *after* the fact, when I see the stack of files, but in the actual moment when I stand up? There’s no anxious monologue happening in my head at all. It’s almost the complete opposite. 

It’s just this... this purely physical thing. Like, I’ll be sitting in my office chair—which, by the way, is one of those really cheap mesh ones they buy in bulk that doesn't even have proper lumbar support, so maybe that doesn't help the situation—but I'll just be sitting there, and my legs will just start to feel kind of... I don't know, tense? Or like there's this weird built-up energy in them that I just can't ignore. And it’s not tied to a specific thought. I could literally be reading the most mundane paragraph about a standard fender bender, completely calm, not a care in the world, and then it’s just like my body makes the decision for me. It’s like a switch flips and my body goes, 'Okay, we are standing up now.' 

And before I even really process what I'm doing, I’m already on my feet and walking toward the breakroom or pacing by the window. So, yeah, looking at it like that, it’s definitely not a worry thing. It’s just this overwhelming physical urge to move my body, stretch my legs, and just be anywhere but in that chair, even though my brain isn't actually panicking or obsessing over anything at all.

Aside from the restlessness, do you currently have trouble staying focused on your claims reviews, frequently losing track of details, forgetting steps, or misplacing paperwork the way you did with worksheets as a child?

Oh man, yeah... it's honestly exactly like the worksheets, just, you know, the adult corporate version of them. It is so frustrating. I mean, my desk is just a complete disaster area most of the time, but even on the days when I actually try to clear it off and get organized, it doesn't even matter because I am constantly hunting for things I literally just had in my hands two seconds ago. 

Like, I’ll print out a physical claim form because sometimes it’s just easier to read the fine print on paper rather than squinting at the dual monitors they give us—which, by the way, one of them has this terrible glare from the overhead fluorescent lights, so I almost have to print things out just to save my eyes. But anyway, I'll be looking right at the claim form, I'll set it down on my desk to type a quick note in the system, and then when I reach for it again, it’s just gone. It’s like it vanished into thin air. I’ll spend ten minutes lifting up manila folders and digging through drawers looking for a piece of paper I just set down.

And it’s not even just the paperwork, either. It’s everything. Like my headset! I have to make these calls to adjusters or auto body shops to verify estimates, and I’ll take my headset off to go get a drink of water or whatever, and when I come back, I have absolutely no idea where I put it. Or I’ll be on a call and I'll scribble down a really important callback number on a sticky note—I even started using the neon pink ones because I figured, hey, they’re bright, I won't lose them, right? But nope. I'll stick it somewhere, and then ten minutes later when I actually need to make the call, I'm tearing my workspace apart hunting for that exact pink sticky note. 

Oh, and my access badge. That is probably the most embarrassing one. You need the badge to get back onto the main processing floor from the breakroom or the bathrooms, and I can't even tell you how many times I've had to just stand there looking like an idiot by the heavy glass doors, waiting for a coworker to happen to walk by and let me back in. And it's all because I took the lanyard off because it was scratching my neck, set the badge down somewhere on my desk, and completely lost it under a pile of files. It’s just exhausting, honestly. I feel like I waste half my day just searching for the basic things I need to actually do my job, and by the time I find whatever it is I lost, I've completely forgotten what I was even supposed to be doing with it in the first place.
